newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels take new town, dent peace optimism.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels take new town, dent peace optimism.

text.p: Zairean rebels captured another town in mineral-rich Shaba province on Friday, foreign sources said, a day after agreeing to hold talks with President Mobutu Sese Seko's shaky regime.
The reported fall of Kasenga was a quick reminder that Laurent Kabila's rebels have a military agenda and are only willing to negotiate the terms of Mobutu's departure.
Kabila controls about a quarter of Zaire, five months after starting the revolt in the east, and his supporters already call him "president".
His and Mobutu's delegates at a summit on the crisis in Togo agreed to hold the first negotiations between the two sides, probably in South Africa early next week.
"It is definitely rebel troops who are in control of Kasenga," an expatriate source in the Shaba capital Lubumbashi with contacts in Kasenga told Reuters.
He said it was a lightning takeover early on Friday and by afternoon the town of about 17,000 people on the Luapula river bordering Zambia was quiet. He and other sources declined to be identified.
Kasenga is on Lake Mweru 220 km (135 miles) north-east of Lubumbashi, Zaire's second city and the centre of the country's colossal reserves of copper, cobalt and precious metals.
There was no immediate confirmation of the fall from the government side, in Lubumbashi or Zaire's capital Kinshasa.

"If nothing changes, then the talks will be in South Africa and will begin on either Monday or Tuesday," Moise Nyarugabo, secretary-general at rebel headquarters, told Reuters in the eastern city of Goma.
In Johannesburg, a government source said the foreign ministry was preparing to host negotiations, likely to take place on Monday or Tuesday.

Nyarugabo said the issue on the table was the transfer of power from the ailing Mobutu to a transitional government led by Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL).
"The principle is the alliance would form the government, it is not a question of power-sharing. Mobutu's party has been in power for 30 years and the results are evident," he said.

Mobutu took power in 1965 with Western backing. His regime degenerated into wholesale corruption, coining the term "kleptocracy". He returned home a week ago, weakened by fresh cancer treatment in Europe.
The rebels insist a ceasefire can be declared only after negotiations have begun.
In the northeast capital of Kisangani, aid workers said more than 75,000 exhausted, hungry and sick refugees were scattered around an 82-km (50-mile) stretch of railway line to the south.
Paul Stromberg, spokesman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, said the Hutu refugees were found on Thursday by aid workers aboard a train carrying food south of the city.

"(At Kasea) I saw the most emaciated people I've ever seen in my life," said a representative of Refugees International on the train. "Many of these people won't last another day without urgent medical attention."
The tens of thousands of Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees are the remnants of 170,000 who fled Tingi Tingi and Amisi this month and have been trekking ever deeper into eastern Zaire.
The foreign sources in Lubumbashi said government troops in Kasenga had fled south and there were wounded people after clashes late on Thursday.

It was unclear whether the clashes involved fighting between the two sides or looting by Zairean troops before they fled southwards towards Lubumbashi, which was bracing itself on Friday for their arrival.
Mobutu's demoralised, unpaid and indisciplined army has never held its ground against the rebels, usually looting and fleeing just before Kabila's men enter a town.

Aides to Kyungu wa Kumwanza told Reuters in Lubumbashi on Friday he had been restored to the governorship of Shaba, formerly called Katanga. He was suspended in 1995, accused of smuggling arms for a secession.
